program: Legal English for International Credit Recovery
hub_subtitle: Do escritório ao tribunal americano — petições, reuniões e o vocabulário do direito civil e empresarial, sem esquecer a vida fora do trabalho

lesson.menu_desc: Preparing a motion with the Miami office and explaining your argument to a U.S. judge: although the defendant..., however..., therefore we request... -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- Writing to the Court
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Caroline Teixeira Nomiyama | Lesson 9 -- Writing to the Court
lesson.grammar_point: linking words of contrast and result: although + sentence, despite + noun / -ing, however (new sentence) x therefore / so (result): Although he was served, he did not answer; therefore, we request a default judgment

listenings.text: Judges are busy people. Although they read every brief, they often have only a few minutes for each one. So my first rule is simple: put your request first. Tell the judge what you want in the first paragraph. Then give the facts, in order, with dates. My second rule is about linking words. Words like however and therefore are not decoration. They show the judge the logic of your argument. However tells the judge: here is the problem. Therefore tells the judge: here is the consequence, and here is what you should do. A clear brief is not a long brief. It's a brief that a tired judge can follow.

Before I moved to New York, I worked as a law clerk for a judge for three years. I used to read every motion and prepare a short summary for her. What surprised me was this: many motions were denied, despite good facts. Why? Because the lawyers didn't explain the risk. They said what happened, but not why the judge had to decide now. The motions that the judge granted always showed three things. First, the facts. Second, the risk: what can happen if the court does nothing. Third, a clear request, in one sentence. Therefore, my advice is simple. Before you file, ask yourself: why now?

I work for a bank in Amsterdam, and we have cases in many countries. When we lose a case, people think we always appeal. We don't. First, my team studies the ruling. An appeal takes time and money, and sometimes the debtor has no assets at all. In that case, even if we win, we recover nothing. Therefore, we don't appeal. Last year, however, we had a different case. Although the first judge ruled against us, the debtor had property in three countries. So we appealed. The higher court changed the ruling, and we recovered most of the money. The lesson: an appeal is a business decision, not only a legal one.
